title: Water Goes Where the Solute Stays

scenes.tts: Here is a puzzle. In the textbook model of an adult man, retain one litre of pure water, with no solute in it. About two thirds of that litre ends up inside cells. Now retain one litre of isotonic saline instead. Once it has spread, none of it ends up inside cells. Same body, same volume. Why does the water go to different places?
scenes.visual: Two litres in the model, one shared between cells and the fluid outside them, one that stays outside: a question mark over where each goes.
scenes.narration: Here is a puzzle. In the textbook model of an adult man, retain one litre of pure water, with no solute in it. About two thirds of that litre ends up inside cells. Now retain one litre of isotonic saline instead. Once it has spread, none of it ends up inside cells. Same body, same volume. Why does the water go to different places?

scenes.tts: First, the tanks. Physiology texts use a seventy kilogram reference man, whose body is sixty percent water. That is a convention for arithmetic, not a measurement of anyone. Total body water is about forty two litres. About two thirds of it, twenty eight litres, is intracellular fluid, the water inside cells. About one third, fourteen litres, is extracellular fluid, the water outside them.
scenes.visual: Body outline holds a 42 L bar that splits into a 28 L inside-cells block and a 14 L outside-cells block.

scenes.tts: Water crosses most cell membranes quickly. So picture two rooms joined by a door that only water can pass. The guests stuck in each room decide how much water it holds. Inside cells, the stuck guests are anions that cannot leave, and the potassium that balances their charge. Outside, they are sodium, with chloride and bicarbonate. Sodium leaks into cells, but the sodium potassium pump moves it back out. So sodium salts are the effective solute of the extracellular fluid.
scenes.visual: Two rooms with a water-only door; stuck solute chips appear in each; water dots pass through the door.

scenes.tts: Now count the guests. In the model, both rooms sit at three hundred milliosmoles per kilogram. These numbers are made up, and rounded. Measured adult values run a little lower. Twenty eight litres of cells hold eight thousand four hundred milliosmoles. Fourteen litres of extracellular fluid hold four thousand two hundred. The model is a closed body, with no urine, sweat or breath losses, and added sodium chloride stays outside cells.
scenes.visual: Both rooms get osmole counts; closed-body assumptions listed.

The model is a closed body, with no urine, sweat or breath losses, and added sodium chloride stays outside cells.

scenes.tts: Retain one litre of isotonic saline. Its particles stay outside, so the concentration does not change. Cells stay at twenty eight litres. Extracellular fluid grows to fifteen. Now retain one litre of solute free water. In the model, it first sits outside cells, so extracellular fluid also reads fifteen. Then water crosses until both rooms match. They end at about two hundred ninety three milliosmoles per kilogram. Cells gain two thirds of a litre. Extracellular fluid gains one third.

scenes.tts: The rule to keep: water follows effective solute. Each compartment holds water in proportion to its effective osmoles. In the model, retained saline stays in the extracellular fluid, because its sodium stays outside. Retained pure water is shared, two thirds to cells. This is equilibrium arithmetic. It predicts where a retained load goes, not how long it stays.
